Trying to Conceive

Understanding a semen analysis: numbers, movement, shape and next steps

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A semen report contains several observations about the fluid and the sperm it carries. A flag beside one number can be unsettling, but it is not a verdict on whether you can have a child. The useful question is how the whole pattern, the way the sample was collected and both partners’ circumstances fit together. This guide explains the main entries and the decisions to discuss with your clinician.

Reference values are a guide, not a fertility score

The World Health Organization’s 2021 reference data describe a group of men whose partners conceived within 12 months. A lower fifth-centile value marks the lower end of that group’s distribution; it does not separate everyone who can conceive from everyone who cannot. Results need the laboratory’s methods and clinical context. A result above every reference value cannot guarantee pregnancy, and one below a value does not rule it out.

NICE’s 2026 guidance uses these lower reference values: volume 1.4 mL; total sperm number 39 million per ejaculate; concentration 16 million per mL; total motility 42%; progressive motility 30%; vitality 54%; and normal forms on morphology assessment 4%. These are different measurements with different units. Older reports and websites may show earlier values, so ask which methods and references your laboratory uses rather than mixing tables.

Check the collection details before interpreting the numbers

Follow your laboratory’s instructions for abstinence, the collection container and delivery. A commonly used abstinence interval is two to seven days. Collect the entire ejaculate and tell the laboratory if any was missed, especially the first portion. Report the collection time, recent fever or illness, medicines and any difficulty producing the sample. A collection problem is useful information, not something to hide.

Ordinary condoms, saliva and unapproved lubricants can interfere with testing. Ask the laboratory about approved alternatives if needed. Do not collect spilled material back into the pot. Home collection may be possible, but timing and transport conditions belong to the receiving laboratory’s instructions. A home sperm-count kit does not necessarily assess the full set of measures discussed here.

Volume: how much fluid was collected

Volume is the amount of semen, measured in millilitres. Semen includes sperm from the testes and fluid from reproductive glands, especially the seminal vesicles and prostate. More fluid does not necessarily mean more sperm: a sample can have a large volume but a low concentration, or contain no sperm despite visible ejaculation.

A low volume may reflect an incomplete sample, some semen passing backwards into the bladder, a duct problem or a hormone problem. The clinician looks at the other findings before deciding what to investigate. Do not use the old 1.5–6 mL range as a universal fertility test, or assume that a high volume proves inflammation. Appearance and quantity alone cannot establish the cause.

Concentration and total number: read the units

Concentration means how many sperm are present in one millilitre. Total sperm number describes the whole ejaculate. For example, a 3 mL sample with 20 million sperm per mL contains about 60 million sperm in total. A report may write millions as 10⁶. Confusing per-millilitre with per-ejaculate values can make the same result seem much better or worse than it is.

A low concentration is often called oligozoospermia. Azoospermia means that no sperm are found after the appropriate laboratory assessment; it does not mean that sperm merely move slowly. Very low or absent sperm needs confirmation and specialist assessment, including consideration of production and blockage problems. Do not choose treatment from a single count or assume that no sperm in one sample means that none can ever be found.

Motility: moving is not the same as moving forward

Total motility includes sperm moving forward and sperm moving without effective forward progress. Progressive motility concerns forward movement, including movement in a broad circular path. Reports may separate faster and slower progression or use abbreviations such as PR for progressive and NP for non-progressive movement. Read the laboratory’s key rather than adding percentages from different categories twice.

The current reference values are 42% for total movement and 30% for progressive movement. A low movement result is described as reduced motility, sometimes called asthenozoospermia. Collection and transport, illness and other reproductive factors can affect the finding. The result does not by itself establish which factor caused it, and low motility is not the same condition as absent sperm.

Vitality: living sperm may be immotile

Vitality estimates the proportion of sperm that are alive. It answers a different question from motility: a sperm that is not moving may still be alive. Laboratories use special tests to make that distinction, particularly when many sperm are immotile. The current lower reference value is 54% living sperm.

Reduced vitality does not necessarily mean every sperm is dead. Ask whether the result could have been affected by collection materials, delay or handling, and whether confirmation is needed. Do not infer sperm survival from the appearance of semen or try to change a laboratory result with a lubricant or supplement. The team interprets vitality alongside movement, number and the rest of the assessment.

Morphology: what the shape percentage means

Morphology is a microscopic assessment of the head, middle section and tail using defined criteria. Under strict methods, only a small proportion may meet every normal-form criterion. The 4% reference value is a proportion of sperm shapes, not a 4% chance of pregnancy and not a measure of the percentage of genetically healthy sperm.

An isolated low morphology result cannot tell you that natural conception is impossible. Equally, normal count and movement do not prove fertility when shape is abnormal. Ask about the method, whether there is a particular severe pattern and how repeat results compare. Morphology helps inform the whole assessment; it does not automatically dictate IVF or ICSI.

Liquefaction and viscosity describe different properties

Fresh semen can be gel-like and then become more fluid. Liquefaction describes that change over time; viscosity describes how thick or resistant to flow the sample remains. These should not be treated as interchangeable entries. Laboratories assess them under controlled conditions, and a report may note delayed or incomplete liquefaction rather than a single pass–fail number.

ASRM laboratory guidance describes allowing 30–60 minutes for liquefaction. Use the laboratory’s actual method and comment rather than diagnosing a gland problem from a home observation. A thick sample is not proof of blockage or infertility. The older suggestion to resolve the question with a postcoital cervical-mucus test is not routine current care: NICE advises against that test for predicting pregnancy.

pH: acidity is interpreted with the rest of the sample

The pH describes how acidic or alkaline the semen is. NICE uses 7.2 or above as a reference. This is a separate type of observation from sperm count or movement, and a pH result does not provide a personal probability of conception. Ask the clinician to explain the laboratory comment rather than trying to alter semen pH yourself.

An acidic sample together with low volume and absent sperm can raise concern about a duct or gland-related problem. That pattern may lead to selected investigations; low pH alone is not enough to diagnose an obstruction. Imaging is chosen for the findings, not automatically ordered for everyone with an out-of-range result.

White cells and round cells need clarification

A report may mention white blood cells, also called leukocytes, or the broader category of round cells. Round cells can include immature germ cells as well as white cells, so further laboratory assessment may be needed. Around one million white cells per mL is an important threshold used in interpretation; the cell type and testing method matter.

Increased white cells can indicate inflammation but do not by themselves prove bacterial infection. Symptoms and further tests guide whether infection treatment is appropriate. Antibiotics are not a way to correct every white-cell flag, and treating white cells alone has not been shown to improve conception. The report cannot establish that a dental problem caused the finding.

What happens after an abnormal result?

Semen measures vary, and one sample may not represent your usual pattern. Ask whether the laboratory recommends confirmation, whether collection conditions should change and when the clinician wants to review you. Bring the complete report rather than only the flagged number. A repeat test is an opportunity to clarify the result, not proof that the first test was useless.

Timing depends on the finding and guidance used. WHO’s 2025 guideline conditionally suggests at least 11 weeks before repeating abnormal parameters, with very low certainty of evidence. NICE recommends about three months ideally, but earlier confirmation for absent sperm or a severe deficiency. Do not postpone an indicated specialist assessment simply to complete a standard waiting interval. If every value is in range, the clinical history can still require investigation.

The assessment looks for causes in the whole clinical picture

Possible contributors include problems with sperm production, reproductive ducts or ejaculation, hormonal or genetic conditions, varicocele, infection, previous treatment and some medicines. Recent illness and sample conditions also matter. Sometimes no single cause is found. A result alone cannot distinguish all of these or tell you that a particular habit is responsible.

A clinician reviews reproductive and medical history and examines you, then chooses tests that could change care. Hormone tests, genetic tests and imaging have specific indications; not everyone needs every test. When relevant, the other partner’s assessment proceeds alongside yours because age, ovulation, tubes and other factors influence the options and timing. An abnormal report should not become a reason to blame either person.

Treat a cause where possible and support general health

Care may involve treating an identified infection or hormone disorder, reviewing a medicine, or considering repair of a suitable varicocele or obstruction. Hormone treatment is selected for a diagnosis, not prescribed to everyone with a low count. Testosterone taken from outside the body can reduce or stop sperm production; do not use it as a fertility booster or stop a prescription without discussing a supervised plan.

Stopping smoking, avoiding recreational drugs and anabolic steroids, moderating alcohol, managing health conditions and reviewing heat or workplace exposures are reasonable topics for the consultation. Improvement is not guaranteed. Supplements marketed for fertility have uncertain benefit and should not postpone assessment. Ask what change is justified, what benefit is realistic and how progress will be assessed.

IUI, IVF and ICSI have different roles

In IUI, a clinic prepares sperm and places the selected sample into the uterus; fertilisation still needs to happen inside the body. Suitability depends on both partners’ findings, and a persistently low number of moving sperm can reduce the chance of success. In IVF, eggs are collected and fertilisation takes place in the laboratory before an embryo is transferred.

ICSI is a technique within IVF in which an embryologist injects one sperm into an egg. It may be useful for particular sperm problems or previous fertilisation failure, but it is not automatically the only option for every low count or poor shape result. It adds procedures and can damage an egg. Discuss the reason for recommending it, alternatives and the prospects for a live birth; successful fertilisation is not a pregnancy guarantee.

Sperm retrieval and donor treatment are individual choices

If suitable sperm cannot be obtained in an ejaculate, a specialist may consider retrieval from the epididymis or testis. The method depends on whether sperm are blocked or poorly produced and on other findings. Some methods use a needle; others involve tissue sampling or microsurgery. A low count or ejaculation difficulty does not automatically require an operation, and retrieval may find no usable sperm.

Retrieved sperm generally need an assisted treatment such as ICSI. Discuss surgical risks, storage plans and what happens if the procedure is unsuccessful before proceeding. Donor sperm may be another option when appropriate, with counselling and local consent, screening and legal requirements. People can also choose to pause or stop treatment. The best plan reflects preferences and the whole assessment, not simply the aim of making every report value normal.

Prepare questions and know when not to wait

For the next appointment, ask which findings are most significant, whether the sample was complete, when to repeat it and which further tests would change the plan. Write down the agreed follow-up date and seek emotional support if the uncertainty is difficult. Do not wait for a repeat semen test to report a new testicular lump, swelling, change in shape or concerning discomfort; obtain urgent medical advice.

Sudden severe testicle pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest needs emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; arrange a safe driver or an ambulance through local emergency services. A semen report, even a reassuring one, cannot rule out an urgent cause of symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the complete report and explain missed sample portions, recent illness, medicines and collection or delivery difficulties.

Ask what needs confirmation, when the clinician wants to review you and which selected tests would change treatment.

Discuss the benefits, risks and alternatives of treatment in the context of both partners, and seek prompt care for new symptoms.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains common report terms and questions to take to a consultation. It cannot interpret an individual sample, diagnose the cause of infertility, predict pregnancy or choose treatment. A note or reminder does not replace the agreed clinical follow-up.

When to seek help

Do not self-prescribe antibiotics, testosterone, fertility medicines or supplements, or stop prescriptions without advice. Seek urgent advice for a new testicular lump, swelling or change. Sudden severe testicle pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or at rest requires emergency assessment; do not drive yourself. A routine repeat-test date must not delay urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Read the whole report with collection details and the clinician’s assessment.
  • Reference values do not divide everyone into fertile and infertile groups.
  • Concentration, total number, movement, vitality and shape answer different questions.
  • White cells do not automatically prove infection, and delayed liquefaction is not the same as viscosity.
  • Repeat timing and treatment depend on the findings; severe results and urgent symptoms should not wait for a routine timetable.

Frequently asked questions

How many sperm should there be in the whole sample?

The current lower reference value is 39 million per ejaculate. This is the total number, not the concentration per millilitre, and it is not a pregnancy guarantee or an absolute infertility boundary. The clinician considers the rest of the report and both partners’ circumstances.

What concentration is used as a reference?

NICE’s 2026 guidance uses 16 million sperm per mL with the relevant WHO methods. Older tables may show 15 million. Check the report’s units and laboratory methods; a small difference around a reference value should not determine treatment by itself.

How much movement is expected?

The current lower reference values are 42% total motility and 30% progressive motility. Total movement includes non-progressive movement; progressive movement describes travel forward. A low movement result is not azoospermia, which means no sperm are found after appropriate assessment.

What does sperm morphology measure?

It assesses shape under defined laboratory criteria. A 4% normal-forms result is not a 4% chance of pregnancy and does not reveal which sperm are genetically healthy. Shape must be considered with the complete semen analysis and clinical assessment.

If sperm do not move, are they all dead?

No. Vitality testing distinguishes living immotile sperm from dead sperm. A low vitality percentage also does not necessarily mean that every sperm is dead. Ask whether the sample needs confirmation and whether collection or handling affected it.

Do white cells or thick semen mean I need antibiotics?

Not automatically. White cells may reflect inflammation without infection, and round cells are not always white cells. Liquefaction and viscosity are separate observations. Symptoms and appropriate tests guide care; do not start antibiotics or another treatment to correct a flag yourself.

Should I always wait three months for another test?

No. Guidance commonly allows time for a new sperm-production cycle, but absent sperm or severe deficiencies can need earlier confirmation and assessment. Agree the timing with the clinician. New symptoms need their own assessment rather than waiting for the next semen sample.

Does an abnormal report mean IVF or surgery is unavoidable?

No. Confirmation, the cause, other reproductive factors and your preferences guide the plan. Options may include treating an identified problem, selected fertility treatment or donor sperm. ICSI and surgical retrieval have specific roles and cannot guarantee a baby; discuss why any proposed procedure is appropriate.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
